title: Land and Real Estate Price Sensitivity to a Disaster: Evidence from the 2011 Thai Floods
question: Did the 2011 Thai floods lower land and real estate prices?
data: JETRO survey land prices for about 40 industrial estates (10 rounds, Oct 2008-Nov 2012); Agency for Real Estate Affairs (AREA) price series for 43 districts in 9 provinces, 2010-2013, by land use and dwelling type
identification: DiD: seven flooded industrial estates vs others (estate FE, pre-trend test); flooded provinces (Ayutthaya, Pathum Thani, Nonthaburi) vs non-flooded provinces (district FE)
main_finding: Industrial land prices fell (8.27% of mean post-flood, JETRO; 6.49% AREA); townhouse prices fell 4.85%; residential and commercial land, detached houses and condominiums showed no significant change. Authors read this as illiquidity or other frictions.
how_my_project_differs: Province-level treatment and district price series only; no hazard (ex-ante) measure, no satellite exposure, no official Treasury appraisal values, no lender valuations. My project moves to parcel/collateral-level exposure and to appraisal and credit outcomes.

title: High water, no marks? Biased lending after extreme weather
question: Do lenders mark collateral valuations to market after a severe flood?
data: 119,239 English properties transacted at least twice around the 2013-14 winter floods; 38,747 refinancing transactions with lender valuation, loan amount and rate; Environment Agency flood outlines and maps; JBA Matrix Scores; postcode-unit level
identification: Repeat-transaction DiD comparing flooded vs unaffected postcode units and sale prices vs refinancing valuations; propensity score matching; postcode-district x year FE
main_finding: Prolonged flooding lowers sale prices by 2.6-4.2% but refinancing valuations do not follow, giving a valuation bias of 2.9-3.2%; loan amounts unaffected; rate response not robust; low-risk borrowers select into high flood-risk areas.
how_my_project_differs: UK, insured market, lender valuations benchmarked to transaction prices. My project would test the same valuation channel in an emerging market with thin insurance, and against official appraisal values as well as lender valuations.

title: Flooded Collateral: Bank Asset Management and Lending Decisions
question: Do banks incorporate flood risk into collateral valuations and lending decisions?
data: Loan and collateral data from one major Belgian bank matched to Flemish government flood-risk maps
identification: 2021 Western European floods as a salience shock (pre/post by exposure of collateral)
main_finding: After the floods, collateral exposed to pluvial or sea-level-rise risk is revalued downward; internal staff account for these risks more than external experts and the bank shifts to internal models; rates rise on floating-rate loans of exposed firms but exposure is not cut.
how_my_project_differs: One bank in a rich country, corporate collateral. My project targets an emerging market and links exposure to PD, LGD and ECL staging rather than valuation alone; the title overlap with 'Underwater Collateral' should be acknowledged.

title: Flood risk information effects on land price fluctuation: Using 'Safety level map of chi-saki' (in Japanese)
venue: Reports of the City Planning Institute of Japan 14(4):276-280
question: Is detailed flood-risk information (Shiga's 2012 'chi-saki' safety map) reflected in land prices?
data: 366 sites of the official Prefectural Land Price Survey (都道府県地価調査) in Shiga, 2012 and 2014; simulated inundation depth for 1/10, 1/100 and 1/200-year rainfall
identification: Cross-tabulation and OLS of 2012 price level and 2012-14 price change on maximum inundation depth plus location controls; no control group or causal design
main_finding: Many sites with inundation potential saw land prices rise; in 2012 deeper 1/10-year inundation depth is positively associated with land price (5% level); the map's publication had very little effect on 2012-14 price changes. Authors call for appraisals to take hazard into account.
how_my_project_differs: Only study found that uses official appraised land values; descriptive, two years, one prefecture, no credit link. My project would use official appraisals with a causal design and connect them to collateral and credit risk.

title: Neglected No More: Housing Markets, Mortgage Lending, and Sea Level Rise
question: How have housing and mortgage markets in coastal Florida responded to sea-level-rise exposure over time?
data: Home transactions (cash and mortgaged), mortgage applications and flood insurance linked to SLR projections at census-tract level, coastal Florida, 2001-2020 (771 tracts within half a mile of the coast)
identification: Matching DiD (synthetic control, nearest neighbour, generalised propensity score) with 2001-2012 baseline; heterogeneity by poverty and climate-concern survey
main_finding: From 2013-2018 sales volumes in the most exposed tracts fell 16-20% relative to matched tracts while prices moved in step; relative prices fell 5-10% below trend by 2020. Little change in loan denial, securitisation or refinancing; authors favour a buyer-demand explanation.
how_my_project_differs: US coastal SLR, transaction data, volumes lead prices. My project asks the parallel question for appraisal values and collateral in an emerging market, where volumes and transaction prices may be thin.

title: The effect of information about climate risk on property values
question: Do US housing markets price flood-zone information?
data: CoreLogic deeds for all US states 1996-2017; FEMA historical (Q3) and current flood maps; compendia of map changes
identification: Panel (same house rezoned into floodplain), DiD on small areas, and cross-section for comparison; heterogeneity by buyer type and state disclosure law
main_finding: Preferred panel estimate of the flood-zone discount is -2.1% (95% CI -4.9% to 0.8%), below the roughly -6.9% implied by insurance costs at a 5% discount rate; larger penalty for commercial buyers and in strict-disclosure states; floodplain homes overvalued by about $34bn in aggregate (WP figure).
how_my_project_differs: Map-revision design on transaction prices in the US. My project would exploit Thai hazard-map or flood-extent information as the shock and use appraisal values in a market without mandatory insurance.

title: Disaster on the horizon: The price effect of sea level rise
question: Are long-horizon sea-level-rise risks priced in US housing?
data: US coastal home sales and rents with SLR exposure (details beyond abstract not read)
identification: Comparison of observably equivalent exposed and unexposed homes equidistant from the beach; rental placebo
main_finding: Exposed homes sell for about 7% less; the discount has grown over time and is driven by sophisticated buyers and communities worried about global warming; no relation with rents; 4% discount for homes not projected to flood for almost a century.
how_my_project_differs: Long-run SLR on transaction prices in the US. My project concerns riverine/pluvial flood exposure and appraisal and collateral values in Thailand.

title: Does Climate Change Affect Real Estate Prices? Only If You Believe In It
question: Do house prices reflect belief differences about climate change?
data: Comprehensive US transaction data with inundation projections for individual homes and measures of climate beliefs
identification: Equilibrium sorting model plus reduced-form comparison of believer and denier neighbourhoods
main_finding: Homes projected to be underwater sell at a discount in believer neighbourhoods relative to denier neighbourhoods.
how_my_project_differs: Beliefs drive capitalisation; Thailand lacks comparable belief data. My project could test whether appraisers (not buyers) update after floods.

title: Is the Risk of Sea Level Rise Capitalized in Residential Real Estate?
question: Is sea-level-rise risk capitalised into coastal house prices?
data: Coastal home sales merged with elevation relative to local tides
identification: Cross-sectional variation in relative SLR from vertical land motion, comparing homes of similar elevation and distance to coast
main_finding: Precisely estimated null results, suggesting limited price effects.
how_my_project_differs: Contrasting null result on SLR; my project focuses on realised and mapped flood hazard and appraisal values.

title: Changes in implicit flood risk premiums: Empirical evidence from the housing market
venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 65(3):361-376
question: How do flood-zone price differentials change around and after major floods?
data: Property sales in Pitt County, North Carolina, around Hurricanes Fran (1996) and Floyd (1999) and a later period
identification: Hedonic DiD across multiple storm events
main_finding: No flood-zone discount before Fran; discounts of 5.7% after Fran and 8.8% after Floyd; 6.0-20.2% premium in later data that diminishes and essentially disappears 5-6 years after Floyd.
how_my_project_differs: Speed and decay of salience on transaction prices in one US county. My project would estimate the same dynamics after the 2011 and later Thai floods on appraisal values.

title: Rising sea levels and sinking property values: Hurricane Sandy and New York's housing market
question: How did Hurricane Sandy affect New York City housing values?
data: Parcel-level NYC sales 2003-2017 with geocoded FEMA damage data
identification: Event study/DiD by flood-zone status and damage
main_finding: Damaged properties fell 17-22% immediately then partially recovered; undamaged flood-zone properties developed a gradual penalty reaching 8% by 2017 with no sign of recovery, consistent with learning.
how_my_project_differs: Separates damage from learning in a rich city. My project would separate physical damage (satellite flood extent) from hazard learning for Thai collateral.

title: Climate Risk and Beliefs in New York Floodplains
venue: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 7(6):1069-1111
question: What are the price effects of insurance reform, a hurricane and new flood maps?
data: Census of NYC residential property transactions 2003-2017
identification: DiD for three flood-risk signals (Biggert-Waters reform, Hurricane Sandy, new floodplain maps) and a model decomposing premium and belief effects
main_finding: All three signals have negative price effects; properties added to the floodplain after escaping Sandy fell 11%; new maps induced belief changes comparable to the insurance reform.
how_my_project_differs: Flood-map disclosure evidence from a high-insurance setting. In Thailand insurance is thin, so belief updating, not premiums, would be the main channel.

title: Is Flood Risk Capitalised Into Property Values?
question: What is the 'best' estimate of the floodplain price discount?
data: Meta-analysis of 37 published works and 364 point estimates
main_finding: Estimates range from -75.5% to +61.0%; coastal floodplain estimates positive, likely due to omitted amenities, with publication bias; time since last flood matters; inland 100-year floodplain discount of -4.6% as a rule of thumb.
how_my_project_differs: Benchmark for magnitudes; my project would add an emerging-market, appraisal-based estimate; the abstract does not say whether the meta-sample contains any.

title: Who Bears Flood Risk? Evidence from Mortgage Markets in Florida
question: Do mortgage lenders screen for uninsurable flood risk?
data: Florida mortgage market data (details beyond abstract not read)
identification: Strict NFIP coverage limits plus staggered flood-map updates
main_finding: Lenders require lower LTVs at origination for uninsurable flood risk; delinquency rates equalise inside and outside flood zones; borrower composition shifts to richer, higher-credit-quality households.
how_my_project_differs: Shows lenders respond through LTV when residual risk is retained. In Thailand most flood risk is uninsured, so my project tests whether LTV, appraisal haircuts or provisioning carry that response.

title: How Responsive Are Mortgage Lending Conditions to Flood Risk? The Case of the Netherlands
question: Do Dutch mortgage terms reflect flood risk?
identification: Cross-sectional comparison of terms by flood-risk area; DiD around the 2021 river flood
main_finding: Credit terms indistinguishable between risk and no-risk areas; after the 2021 flood lenders temporarily (about six months) raised rate premiums and partly reduced LTVs.
how_my_project_differs: Securitised loan terms in a rich country. My project looks at bank-held collateral, appraisal values and provisioning in an emerging market.

title: The Effect of Flood Risk on Residential Land Prices
question: Is flood risk capitalised into residential land prices in Hangzhou?
data: 424 residential land plot transactions 2007-2020 from the China Land Market Network, date-adjusted with an official land price index; 2017 municipal flood-risk assessment map (four risk classes)
identification: Spatial Durbin model (cross-sectional hedonic with spatial lags)
main_finding: High-flood-risk plots sell at an 8.62% discount ceteris paribus; non-spatial OLS gives a positive flood coefficient; authors argue government benchmark land prices already account for flood hazard.
how_my_project_differs: Emerging-market land evidence but cross-sectional, state land sales, no event or credit link. My project uses a time-varying flood shock and links to collateral and credit.

title: Putting a Price on Safety - a Hedonic Price Approach to Flood Risk in African Cities
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10127
question: Is flood risk reflected in rents in four Sub-Saharan African cities?
data: Household surveys after floods in Accra, Antananarivo, Dar es Salaam and Addis Ababa; self-reported past exposure and perceived risk
main_finding: Flood risk associated with 14-56% lower rents in Accra, Antananarivo and Addis Ababa; positive in Dar es Salaam; only 12% of households in flood-prone areas knew the risk when they moved in.
how_my_project_differs: Emerging-market evidence on rents with self-reported risk. My project uses satellite-measured exposure and collateral/appraisal values.
